en: Śrī.
The Mānasollāsa composed by King Śrī Someśvara.
The Third Part:
Bhūlokamalla-deva describes that which is based on song:
one who is free from disease, of sound mind, having accomplished his purpose, and possessed of great wealth.
Satisfied and joyful in mind, he ought to find diversion in song;
he is a lover of the beautiful, a hero in generosity, and one who knows the true essence of the meaning of all the scriptures.
He was solely devoted to virtue, averse to slander,
mature, pleasant-spoken, eloquent, wise, and a discerning knower of distinctions.
He was skilled in discerning gestures, knew the vital points of others, possessed discrimination, and was greedy for fame;
he was proficient in the arts of singing and instrumental music, and expert in the rhythms of dance.

One who knows the investigation of regional and classical musical styles shall become a king or a presiding officer of an assembly; those who know the true principles of the three types of instruments are connoisseurs who cherish virtuous qualities.
They were speakers appropriate to the occasion, free from passion and hatred,
cognizant of inner dispositions and the hearts of others, and proficient in all languages.
They were most righteous, embodied, youthful, and endowed with genius;
they were worthy of honor, possessed of knowledge, and conversant with poetry and drama.
Such members are praised in debate as well as in recreation;
having thus invited such members, one should take one's seat in the assembly hall, in the portico.
The king should seat them upon appropriate seats,
followed by his most beloved consorts, who captivate the heart and the eye.
Rich in gestures, emotions, and amorous play, they bring about the festival of love;
these passionate women, full of delight, are playful and graceful.
Having summoned his beloved women— those with slender waists, broad hips, and full, rounded breasts— he should seat them at his sides and behind him.
He [placed] his sons— who were skilled in the arts, connoisseurs of aesthetic flavor, and endowed with learning—
in front, in the winged section, amidst the members of the assembly.
One should employ them for the sake of training, for diversion, and for delight;
and from that, one should produce vocal compositions (gāyana) that are superior, inferior, or middling.
Having identified various singers— whether excellent, mediocre, or inferior—
as well as those who have become like fire [in their intensity] and those skilled in the art of instrumental music,
he should, through his overseers, station them in their appropriate places.
The lowest is the maker of the mother; the middling is the maker of the element;
the one who performs the action of both the element and the mother is proclaimed as the most excellent.
He who composes a work that is merely strung together, devoid of the element of passion (rāga),
and lacking in dignity (māna), is considered the lowest of lyric poets.
One whose intellect is utterly deluded does not know how to properly subdue passion;
merely occupied with material objects, he is declared to be the lowest of men.
The mediocre singer endows the musical element (*dhātu*) joined with passion (*rāga*) with the proper characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*),
yet he does not understand the underlying meaning (*padārtha*) of the song.
He who generally composes long compositions endowed with both *dhātu* (etymology) and *mātu* (prosody),
yet does not truly understand them, is also called mediocre.
He was proficient in the science of grammar as well as in the path of poetics;
he was skilled in the treatises on the arts and adept in worldly affairs.

He was proficient in the treatises on music, a knower of the characteristics and definitions of musical notes, and skilled in the primary and secondary melodies, the dialects, and the various musical performances.
He is the author of all compositions and is expert in the analysis of the elements and their constituents.
He is the creator of all methods and is proficient in the languages of every country.
Skilled in the measurement and performance of rhythmic time (tāla), fearless and endowed with creative genius,
he quickly composes the song and sings it in accordance with its melody.
Skilled in the application of vocal modulations and in the composition of verses,
this preeminent singer is said to be the most excellent of the excellent.
Even if he is deficient in certain qualities, one who is expert in the elements and their proportions should be recognized as the best by those proficient in the science of singing.
One who produces a sound devoid of correct pitch, who has not mastered the three places of articulation,
and who has lost his place [of voice] should be known as a singer utterly despised by other singers.

He should be known as an *apasvara*, a censured and most wretched singer; he is a sinner, offensive to the ear, and a destroyer of those who live by the *rāgas*.
He in whom a deficiency or excess of pitch is perceived among the notes beginning with Ṣaḍja,
should be known as an outsider, censurable, a singer who destroys the *rāga*.
That singer who sings by means of the sounds arising from the nostrils should be known as Kapila; he, too, is considered the most difficult [to master].
Bearing a face shaped like a gourd, filled with air and sealed shut,
emitting but a slight sound, the tumbakī is the lowest of singers.
He whose voice is like the cawing of a crow, harsh to the ear, and whose resonance falters during recitations— he who possesses such a "crow-like" voice is severely censured.
He who sings while biting all his teeth as if chewing the sequence of words should be known as "sandasta," a destroyer of song.
But he who sings what has been established as fixed in a manner that is unfixed is called an "unfixed" singer and is censured by the wise.
A singer who repeatedly utters hissing sounds with frequent inhalations and exhalations,
accompanied by coughing and spitting, is the lowest of singers.
He on whose neck and forehead a network of veins is visible,
whose nose is flared, and whose eyes are reddish— he is a censurable jackal.
He who sings while excessively twisting his neck and does not know how to sing evenly is called the "crooked" (vakrī) singer, the lowest of all.
He who, with mouth wide open and accompanied by the sound of *kalāla*, sings a song (*gāthā*) should be known as Karālī; he is to be rejected.

One who closes both eyes and does not see those standing before him, yet sings while being blameless—he is to be known as a praiseworthy singer; one who sings while having his eyes closed [but seeing] is censured.
He who sings while standing on the ground with his neck arched like that of a camel and resting on his knees should be known as the censurable "Camel-necked" (Uṣṭragrīva).
One who stretches out his limbs and hands while singing, being unskilled and singing with excessive pride, is called a *prasārī*; he is not praised.
He whose jaw is drooping and whose throat is like that of a goat— or whose throat is like a goat's—
is blameworthy and fit for ridicule; he is known by the name Udvanda.
That sound which is tremulous and natural in the act of singing is to be known as "trembling" (kampita),
and it is censured by those expert in the science of sound.
He who, having ascended to a high position, is unable to maintain it and gradually falls away, is devoid of resonance and is censured.
When the sound, having become faltering, does not produce the manifestation of the phonemes, it should be known as "indistinct" (avyakta); the wise censure such [recitation].
When the sound of the *vadyaskra* (tuning peg) is rubbed against its back and becomes harsh,
it should be known as "rubbed away" (*utkṛṣṭa*); the wise censure such a lute.
But that singer who, being blameless and dependent on natural physical endowment, sings even difficult songs through practice— he is indeed a mediocre singer.
He whose physical form is beautiful and whose singing is exceedingly straightforward,
yet whose mastery of the song is uneven, is also proclaimed as a Madhyama singer.
The singer who employs notes that are easy on the throat, expressive, short, and free from defects in a clear melody is considered a mediocre singer.
Even one of middling physical strength does not know how to compose extensive literary works, even if he possesses the necessary aids such as time, wealth, and action.
That which manifests the passions even without practice,
being produced together with the body, is called "bodily" (śārīra).
Just as fragrance is in the campaka flower, as luster is in pearls,
and as sweetness is in the stalk of sugarcane, so too is gentleness inherent in his body.

Through the practice performed in other births, through the yoga of knowledge, and through the worship of Śiva, the bodily [state] is attained by means of merits; it is not obtained merely through repeated practice.
He who sings alone, independent of others, with beautiful melody and according to the technical characteristics, is known as a *gāyaka*; if there are two, they are considered *yamalaka*s.
That singer who sings by joining with many others is a group-singer (vṛndagāyaka); among them, each preceding one shall be superior.
The Śikṣaka, the Bhāvaka, the Rañjaka, and likewise the Rasika;
the fifth, known as the Kuṭakāra, has been declared by the wise.
One who recites the Veda, grasping it quickly and without omission, remaining attentive and not forgetting it, is called a teacher of the Śikṣā.
And when there is a loss of rasa, one should unify it by means of the determinants (vibhāvas) and bring forth the emotion (bhāva).
For that egoity (ahaṅkāra), through its cleverness, is called the "evoker" (bhāvaka) of the emotion.
Having understood the hearts of the listeners and according to their mental dispositions,
he who delights them by singing is known as a "delighter" (rañjaka).
Upon hearing a sweet account of himself, he becomes intensely filled with joy;
with his entire body marked by horripilation, such a singer is known as a *rasika*.
That skillful person who perfectly imitates the songs of others, along with their vocal modulations and gestures, is called a "counterfeiter" (kūṭakāra).
Skilled in various forms of discourse, proficient in the release from the [mental] grasp,
capable of attaining the application of the three stations, and having overcome all fatigue.
He possesses well-proportioned neck-lines under his own control, has a fine posture, is devoted to ritual action,
is skilled in the arrangement of his shoulders, is eloquent, and is free from fear.

He was an expert in uneven and smooth songs, in musical compositions, and in all stylistic modes; he was proficient in the art of rhythm and tempo, and possessed knowledge of the application of tempo and release.
The excellent practitioner, skilled in employing the sevenfold classification of *gamaka*,
is one who utilizes sounds produced from the vocal organs beginning with the navel.
Having reached the second note, it repeatedly returns;
when filled with a velocity three times faster [than the previous], they know this as *gamaka*.
If one should likewise turn it back with twice the speed of the quick [turn],
those who know song call that "the Trembling" (*kampita*), which is capable of conveying the meaning.
One should repeatedly cause it to flow back smoothly with a quick tempo;
that which is thus dissolved is called *gamaka* by those expert in the science of song.
If, having reached the third note,
it returns again to its own place with a light measure, they call that the *āndolita* (swaying) rhythm.
If, having traversed three *śrutis*, one moves swiftly [to the next],
that is called *tiripa* by those who know song as a mode of modulation (*gamaka*).
If one strikes a preceding note and quickly returns to its own place,
those skilled in the *gamakas* and other ornaments call this the *āhūta-gamaka*.
That which comes and goes rapidly three times sevenfold is to be known as *tribhinna*, a *gamaka* by those skilled in song.
The path of that [practitioner] proceeds from the location of the navel;
the navel-abiding means of expression (gamaka) should be known as situated in the body, arising from the heart.
That which arises in the region of the throat is employed in the various musical applications;
one should know that the *gamaka* resides in the throat, while the *mudraka* is located in the mouth when it is closed.
He who sings a song endowed with such indicative applications arising from the heart is one possessed of the path of practice.
The singer who, having mastered the resonance, sings a smooth song,
should be known as the best among singers— one who is proficient and endowed with the power of retention.
Having restrained his breath for a very long time, he sings a pervasive resonance;
renowned as the supreme singer, he is endowed with his own power in song.
Skilled in the arts of *laya* and *tāla*, demonstrating the junctions of instrumental music,
he sang with rhythmic pauses and measured tempo, his head shaking in time, while moving within the domain of the Kukkura lineage.
He who clearly unites the three— pitch, syllables, and rhythm—
in a combination of beautiful sound, is indeed a skillful singer.
He who sings according to the application of the treatises and in accordance with the path,
free from defects, is said to be devoted to the ritual action (kriyā).
A sound resembling that of a flute or a lute is considered the "consonant" (dhvani);
one resembling the song of the cuckoo is called the "sweet" (madhura) sound.
That essence of sound which is audible even from a high position and is smooth is considered *snigdha* (smooth).
That sound which is not thin, but rather dense and compact, is declared to be *ghana* (compact).
That sound which is heard whether situated at a distance or even standing in the midst of a crowd,
and which is endowed with qualities such as sweetness, is declared to be the *śrāvaka* tone.

That which is audible even from a high place, beautiful, and endowed with auspicious characteristics is declared to be the best among sounds— the sound that is beautiful in its resonance and placement.

Who is that supreme singer— one whose song is endowed with distinguished sounds from the three registers and musical modulations (gamakas), and who is perfected in both technique and physical execution?
Free from all defects, adorned with certain virtues,
a singer endowed with a perfect body and skillful in performance— he is the most excellent of the excellent.
Physical excellence, purity of sound, maturity, skill in modulation,
knowledge of rhythm, and fearlessness— these are the seven great qualities of a singer.
He likewise appointed excellent flute-players (vaṃśakarās), superior drummers (pāṇavikas),
the finest players of the ḍhakkā drums,
as well as other intermediate players of the mṛdaṅga drums.
Having thus identified those who are experts in singing and instrumental music,
one should cause them to enter and settle in their appropriate places.
Others were skilled in the arts of charm, entirely free from all faults,
proficient in the arts of song and dance, and experts in the science of instrumental music.
In front should be the singer of the *vāggeya* songs; on both sides, the excellent singers;
and behind them, standing nearby, the flute-players endowed with the proper characteristics.
Behind them should be stationed female singers of sweet voice,
who are free from all defects and endowed with beauty and youth.
Behind all of them should be stationed the pāṭahikas and others;
having thus arranged everyone, the song then proceeds.
The coordination of notes, words, and rhythms is called *gīta* (song);
*tāla* (rhythm) would be that which consists of rhythm alone, devoid of words.
Exquisite with its uninterrupted flow of rasa, embellished by the expression of various emotions (bhāvas),
worthy of being heard, heart-pleasing, and free from agitation— such is called the highest form of song.
Teachers desire equanimity; the wise clearly desire what is manifest;
women desire what is sweet; and other men desire what is remote.
Heroes desire [stories] full of enthusiasm; those afflicted by separation, compassion;
parasites, those rich in jesting; and yogis, that which is connected to the inner self.
Full of festive joy, they sang auspicious songs and hymns endowed with devotion; the instrumentalists played music that was mostly complex and characterized by mature rhythmic progression.
Endowed with high and low pitches, neither too fast nor too slow,
sung with equal rhythmic beats, such a song is dear to the teacher.
Endowed with the proper application of grammatical relations and case functions, free from defects of euphonic combination,
and possessed of clearly articulated vowels— this is what is recognized as clear by the learned.
It is composed of graceful and well-joined syllables, colored by the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa);
it is pleasant to hear, endowed with melodic resonance, sweet, and dear to women.
That song which is endowed with increasingly higher notes, developed through various musical applications, and extended in range is called *vikṛṣṭa*; it is enchanting to others.
A description of heroic combat with intense *ārabhaṭī* action,
accompanied by songs in high and low tones, full of enthusiasm, and dear to the wielder of the trident.
It is joined with the words "joy" and "lamp," adorned with the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa),
endowed with the expression of compassion, compassionate, and fond of separation.
Accompanied by a retinue and [expressions of] laughter, augmented by the fortune of others,
this song is noble in its sentiment of humor, full of jesting, and dear to the *viṭas*.
That song, composed of words with hidden meanings and ultimate truths that disparage the pleasures of saṃsāra, was profound and beloved by yogis.
This auspicious song, composed in the pure Pañcama rāga and endowed with beautiful words, should be sung at festivals such as weddings; it is pleasing to women and brings good fortune.
This song of praise, joined with the glorification of the deities, awakening to their power,
generating faith, and dear to the devotees, is a hymn.
A song that is performed in an excessively high register, unmarked by rhythmic beats (tāla), characterized by excessive technical display, harsh, and irregular, is pleasing only to instrumentalists.

A song that possesses a proper place, is simple, pleasant to hear, pure, adorned with modulations of voice (*kāku*), has excellent proportions, and follows the correct sequence is dear to mature persons.
One should [draw] the bitter punishment, endowed with the letters na, ña, ṭa, ḍa, ha, and kṣa,
joined with the letters of the name, and combined with the vowels ā, e, i, u, and ī.
Adorned with notes joined in the low, middle, and high registers,
it is likewise characterized by sustained notes, shifting notes, and both ascending and descending melodic movements.
They praise that supreme *ālapti* which is struck clearly, free from defects, endowed with the various modes of expression prescribed by rule, radiant, and possessing a subtle resonance.
The king should listen to songs composed of various musical structures, produced with diverse melodies, and accompanied by various rhythmic beats.
The king, possessing a beautiful voice, bold and deeply connoisseur of aesthetic flavor (rasika),
should himself sing for his own pleasure or for the delight of his beloveds.
Having sat down and heard the song composed by the singers,
one should then examine the subject matter consisting of the notes, rhythms, and words.
The modulation (*kāku*) that distinguishes the *ṣāḍava*, *auḍuva*, and *pūrṇa* melodies,
as well as the determination of the notes excluding the *graha*, *aṃśa*, and *nyāsa*.
A king who does not know the characteristics (lakṣaṇa) associated with the objects to be characterized (lakṣya) is called ignorant by those who know; he is also an object of ridicule.

The characteristics of sentiments (rāga), poetic expressions (bhāṣā), commentaries (vibhāṣā), and the constituent elements of action (kriyāṅga) should be known; therefore, I shall describe their defining marks for the sake of aesthetic delight.

From the Samaveda the notes (svaras) were born; from the notes the scales (grāmas) arose; from the scales the melodic types (jātis) were born; and from the melodic types the determination of the ragas was established.
From the Rāgas likewise came the Bhāṣās; from the Bhāṣās, the Vibhāṣakas;
and from the Vibhāṣās were born the Antarabhāṣikas.
Indeed, the regional melodies (deśīrāgas) that originate from the names of various regions continue even now,
being most enchanting during musical diversions.
Passion increases through hearing, and the mind is constantly colored by it; therefore, they are called "passions" (rāgas). I shall now state them by name.
There is one called Śuddhaṣāḍava, and likewise another, Śuddhapañcama;
also the so-called Śuddhasādhīra, and Śuddhakaiśikamadhyama.
Śuddhakaiśika—these five are proclaimed as the pure (śuddha) [melodies]. Now listen as I shall proclaim the names of the differentiated (bhinna) ones.
Bhinna-ṣaḍja, Bhinna-tāla, Bhinna-kaiśikamadhyama,
the one known as Bhinna-pañcama, Pañcama, and Bhinna-kaiśika.
One is called Gauḍapañcama, another is Gauḍakaiśikamadhyama, and yet another is Gauḍakaiśika;
these three are proclaimed as the Gauḍa [melas].
Ṣāḍava, Voḍarāga, as well as Mālavapañcama;
Ṭakka, Kaiśika, Sauvīra, and likewise Mālavakaiśika.
Hindola, Ṣaḍja, and Kārṣika—these are the eight rāgas;
thereafter, I shall describe the sādhāraṇas by name, so listen.
Nartarāga, Śaka, Koha, as well as Bhrammaṇa as the fifth,
Rūpasādhārita, and likewise Gāndhārapañcama.
The one known as Ṣaḍjakaiśika—these seven are remembered as the common (sādhāraṇa) [notes]. All these rāgas have been declared by name, as propounded by the Sage.

Those things which are not employed in diversion do not require a definition; therefore, no definition is sought for them. However, the definition of those things which are employed in diversion is now stated.
It is endowed with the ṣaḍja partial tone (aṃśa) and the final cadence (nyāsa), complete with all seven notes;
it is oscillated in its own place and enters accompanied by ṛṣabha.
Even in the descending scale, the Gāndhāra note is employed here and there;
and this Śrīrāga is proclaimed to have a weak Gāndhāra.
This is the characteristic mark of the Gauḍa rāga: Ṛṣabha does not enter here;
and this [note] is sung by those learned in song as being struck in its own place.
The *rāga* beginning with *ṣaḍja* and devoid of *niṣāda* is called *madhyamakampita*;
however, the *somarāga*, which is hexatonic (*ṣāḍava*), contains *gāndhāra* in its descent (*avaroha*).
In the Nyāsa of Aṃśa, the Ṣaḍja is joined with Niṣāda and Ṛṣabha;
it is oscillated in its own place and trembles in the Gāndhāra.
Complete with all seven notes, adorned with the *maṇḍra* and *tāra* registers,
this *rāga* known as Mālavakaiśika was proclaimed by King Soma.
With Ṣaḍja as its partial note (aṃśa), abundant in Ṣaḍja, adorned with a final cadence (nyāsa) on Ṣaḍja, and rich in sound (nāda),
this excellent Harṣapurī is known as being without support (nirālambā).
The Ṣaḍja note shines forth equal to the Niṣāda of the Ṛṣabha;
when oscillated in its own place, it transcends and reaches the Madhyama.
It always occurs in the fifth and the middle [note], and not from any other;
this excellent Hindolaka is renowned for being complete with all the notes (svaras).
With Ṣaḍja as its partial note (aṃśa), struck in its proper place, and always devoid of Ṛṣabha;
it ascends by leaping over Gāndhāra and is shaken by a deep-toned Dhaivata.
By means of the sequence of ascent, it touches slightly upon the fifth [note];
this is proclaimed as the *ṣāḍava* form of the *deśī-hindola*.
It has Dhaivata as its tonic (aṃśa), leading note (graha), and final note (nyāsa); it is complete (saṃpūrṇa) and consists of equal notes (samasvara).
It is oscillated (āndolita) in its own place and mixed with Pañcama.
The Gāndhāra note is tremulous in the low register, and the Ṛṣabha is also tremulous;
the Mairavī [tāna] is proclaimed as being rich in Niṣāda and Ṣaḍja.
With Dhaivata as its primary note (aṃśa), it is similar to that [Rāga], yet it is devoid of Ṣaḍja and Pañcama;
struck in its own position, this Mallāra is thus renowned.
The Māllārī rāga of this very kind, weakened in the notes Ṣaḍja and Pañcama,
is sung in its complete form with a tremolo (kampita) applied to the appropriate notes, in accordance with its defining characteristics.
When there is a *nyāsa* on *dhaivata*, the *śānta* [mūrcchanā] shall be tremulous (*prakampitā*) in its own place;
in *niṣāda* and *madhyama*, it is always [the *nirīpā*], joined with trembling.
The *Sauvīrī* [mūrcchanā] begins with *ṣaḍja*, is devoid of the fifth note (*pañcama*), and consists of *tāra-ṣaḍja*, *madhyama*, and *ṣaḍja*; it vibrates throughout its entire range.
It is joined with a placement of the fifth note, beautified by a slight gāndhāra,
tremulous in its own place, and resplendent with a deep-toned ṣaḍja.
Perfectly complete, possessing the *satiripa* [measure], and endowed with an abundance of *nāda*,
that beautiful style originating from the Andhra country is celebrated as *sāndhālī*.
With the sixth note (dhaivata) as the starting and struck notes, constantly shaken by the fifth (pañcama),
and complete with all the notes, it is known by the name Bhairavī.
The Bangāla rāga is complete, characterized by a placement of the fifth note (pañcama) in the lower register (mandra), adorned with ṛṣabha,
and featuring a pressed-down niṣāda.
The *devāla* scale is based on the fifth-note extraction (*pañcamāṃśagraha*), is weak in *ṣaḍja* and *gāndhāra*,
complete in its notes, and tremulous in *niṣāda* and *ṛṣabha*.
In this [raga], there is karuṇa, kampita, sthāna, sampūrṇa, and tāraśobhita;
likewise, there is durbala, madhyama, and gāndhāramandraka.
In this [raga], the ṛṣabha is indeed afflicted while the niṣāda and ṣaḍja are predominant;
it was named Karṇāṭabaṅgāla by King Soma.
The rāga known by the name Gurjarī is complete, characterized by the *ṛṣabha* and *aṃśa* notes, lacking *gāndhāra* and *dhaivata*, and featuring a trembling *niṣāda*.
The Deśī rāga, beginning with Ṣaḍja, having Dhaivata as its aṃśa and nyāsa and being devoid of Pañcama,
is sung by the learned as being in the ṣāḍava (six-note) scale.
Saurāṣṭrī has Ṣaḍja as its aṃśa, graha, and nyāsa; it is not devoid of Niṣāda, is lacking Madhyama, and is constantly tremulous (kampita).
The Kāmbojī is considered by the wise to be accompanied by the fifth note, Niṣāda, both in the high and low registers, characterized by an upward movement, and devoid of Dhaivata and Ṛṣabha.
Complete with the notes beginning with Ṣaḍja, and vibrating in its own place,
the Madhyama note constantly throbbing— this is remembered as the Punnāṭaka rāga.

The rāga known as Nāgadhvani is characterized by the shaking of the sixth note (ṣaḍja) in its place, is devoid of the fifth (pañcama) and the second (ṛṣabha), and abounds in the third (gāndhāra) and the middle (madhyama).
The fifth [note] is omitted in the nyāsa; it is devoid of ṛṣabha;
being hexatonic (ṣāḍava) and characterized by a trembling [placement], it is sung as Gurjara, and not as Mālava.
With its fifth note fully complete, adorned with tāra-gāndhāra,
having ṣaḍja as its lowest note (mandra) and madhya-ṛṣabha, it is indeed known by the name Kauśikī.
It vibrates in the positions beginning with Ṣaḍja, it is shaken by the deep-toned Dhaivata,
it abounds in the sound of Gāndhāra, and it is complete with all seven notes.
Niṣādadrubalā should be performed with Ṣaḍja and Gāndhāra as the high notes;
it is to be known as Śuddhāvarāṭī by those who understand the characteristics of rāgas.
Complete with the notes beginning with Ṣaḍja, yet weak in Pañcama,
that Karṇāṭavarāṭī should be performed with a slight degree of *sampratipāda*.
It has Ṣaḍja as its partial note (aṃśa) and Ṣaḍja as its final note (tārā), is graced by a nyāsa on Ṣaḍja,
contains very little Pañcama, abounds in Niṣāda, and is excellent.
When it is struck predominantly in the middle Gāndhāra by means of the Ṛṣabha [note],
being endowed with these characteristics, it is considered Varāṭī-Drāviḍī.
With the middle note as the primary interval and its placement, when struck in its own position,
and abounding in Niṣāda and Ṣaḍja, it is proclaimed as the pure Nāṭī.
The Ḍavitā, known as Paurā, is considered to have Dhaivata as its aṃśa, graha, and nyāsa; it is devoid of Pañcama and Ṛṣabha, has Ṣaḍja as its mandra, and possesses Tāra [Ṣaḍja].
Endowed with the characteristics of a nāṭī and trembling in its own place,
it is renowned as Megharāga and is called Trāvaṇī by the wise.
When the fifth part is seized and placed in its position, it becomes oscillating;
devoid of Niṣāda and Tiripa, that Hīrī brings about strife.
It has Dhaivata as its primary note (aṃśa), is concluded with that same note (nyāsa), is constantly shaken by Pañcama,
abounds in Ṣaḍja and Ṛṣabha, and is graced by a high-pitched Gāndhāra.
Joined with the *mandra-madhyama* and pressed by the *ṛṣabha*,
it is called *chāyānāṭī* on earth by King Soma.
Its placement consists of the middle notes, it is complete with all seven notes,
it is always tremulous on the fifth note, and it is adorned by the deep-toned gāndhāra.
From Ṣaḍja, R̥ṣabha, Gāndhāra, Niṣāda, and [Dhaivata]— with R̥ṣabha being most predominant—
it is renowned by the name Dvīti (or Ḍīti), arising from the pure hexatonic scale (śuddha-ṣāḍava).
Toḍikā is that [rāga] which has a complete middle octave (madhyamāṃśa), is intensified by niṣāda and ṛṣabha,
is weak in gāndhāra, and is struck with the ṭī-ṭu-kī rhythm.
That which possesses the nyāsa on the middle note (madhyamā), has the same notes as Ṣaḍjamandra,
and abounds in Dhaivata, is considered to be the Dullītoḍī rāga.
The Vallī ṣāḍava scale is formed by the omission of the middle note (madhyama), the third (gāndhāra), and the fifth (pañcama),
and it abounds in the note dhaivata.
With Dhaivata as its *aṃśa* (concluding note) and *graha* (opening note), it is complete;
it should be oscillated in its [proper] place and enriched with the pressure and trembling of Ṣaḍja; this is called the Bahurīti.

It has Dhaivata as its tonic (aṃśa), keynote (graha), and final note (nyāsa); it is always characterized by a trembling of the Ṣaḍja note, joined with a deep-toned Gāndhāra, and likewise abounds in Niṣāda.
Filled with all seven notes and pressed by the sharp (tāra) pañcama,
this rāga is celebrated as Velāvalī by King Soma.
Endowed with these characteristics, and featuring the notes Ṣaḍja, Gāndhāra, Dhaivata, and Pañcama, this rāga is called Chāyāvelāḍallī; it is complete with all seven musical notes.
With Dhaivata as its tonic (aṃśa), dominant (graha), and final (nyāsa) notes, and devoid of Madhyama,
it is proclaimed by the name Cuṅghī, characterized by a tremolo on Ṣaḍja and Pañcama.
That [rāga] which has Dhaivata as its *aṃśa*, *graha*, and *nyāsa*, which vibrates in the low (*mandra*) and middle (*madhya*) registers,
and is joined with Niṣāda as the high (*tāra*) note, is proclaimed as Haṃsa.
With Ṣaḍja as its *aṃśa*, Dhaivata as its *nyāsa*, and being weak in Pañcama, it is rich in the trembling of Dhaivata and Ṛṣabha; indeed, that is known by the name Khaṃbhārī.
When it begins with the note Dhaivata, concludes with a Nyāsa on that same note, is complete, tremulous,
and possesses both high (tāra) and low (mandra) Gāndhāra notes, it is proclaimed as Kāmodā.
The Sīṃhalī rāga is known as Kāmodā, having Dhaivata as its aṃśa, graha, and nyāsa; it is trembled by Pañcama, complete with all the notes, and is thus remembered.
The *grahas* are *aṃsa*, *nyāsa*, and *gāndhāra*; in the place of the *graha*, there is *sakampita*.
With *ṛṣabha* and others as the *ādi*, it is very high (*atitāra*); this is known by the name *deśāṅka*.
Containing the Ṣaḍja as its partial tone (aṃśa), its primary note (graha), and its final cadence (nyāsa), and being devoid of Dhaivata and Ṛṣabha;
with Niṣāda as its low pitch (mandra) and Śrutārā as its characteristic, it is indeed known by the name Nandāśrī (or Dhanāśrī).
The Lalita is considered to be a Ṭauḍuvitā (Ṭauḍava), having Dhaivata and Niṣāda as its Aṃśas and Samvādins, being accompanied by Mandra, slightly touching Pañcama, and devoid of Niṣāda and Gāndhāra.
With the middle note as the first and with the fifth and ṛṣabha notes omitted,
this is called Kolāhalā by King Somabhūpa.
Dhaivatī is proclaimed as having Dhaivata as its tonic (aṃśa), its graha, and its nyāsa; it is devoid of Pañcama and Ṛṣabha, is exalted by Gāndhāra and Madhyama, and contains Niṣāda and Dhaivata.
Those who know the system recognize that *ḍombakṛti* has Dhaivata as its *aṃśa*, *graha*, and *nyāsa*; it is tremulous in its own place (*nijasthāna*) and devoid of Pañcama and Ṛṣabha.
The Rāmā (or Ramakṛti) is considered to be characterized by the use of Ṣaḍja as its *aṃśa* and *nyāsa*, devoid of Pañcama,
possessing a soft (*samandra*) quality, with Ṛṣabha as its preeminent note, and being delightful.
Having Ṣaḍja as its partial note (aṃśa), enriched by Ṛṣabha, and devoid of Dhaivata;
trembling in its own place, it is known by the name Tuṇḍakṛti.
The characteristics of the *rāgas* have now been declared by me in brief;
hereafter, the characteristics of the musical compositions (*prabandhas*), together with their names, shall be stated.

Where the object to be defined (lakṣya) is understood through the definition (lakṣaṇa) of the compositions, no separate illustrative example (udāhṛti) is stated; it is said that [an example] is mentioned only when there is a need for dependence [on further clarification].
The various classes of meters (vṛttajātayaḥ) are sung with the placement of musical notes (svaranyāsa) at the end of each foot;
they have no restriction of tempo (tāla), and among them, the meter (chandas) is the primary factor.
Therefore, having provided examples through metrical patterns according to the count of syllables, morae, and so forth, I shall explain the determination of the divisions of those meters.
The sixth syllable is heavy everywhere, and the fifth is light;
in the even [pādas], there is a *la* (light syllable) at the seventh—this is stated to be the definition of a *śloka*.
Salutations to Him whose sole emblem is Garuḍa, the cause of all perfections, the cause for the destruction of impurities, and the bridge across the ocean of worldly existence.

The syllable *ma* with three heavy (long) vowels bestows wealth; *ya* brings prosperity; *va* or *ca*, being light in the middle, indicates water; *ra* in the middle indicates fire; *sa* at the end indicates wandering through foreign lands;
*ta* with a light vowel at the end indicates the loss of wealth; *ja* in the middle indicates the sun; and *ru* in the middle indicates disease.
May the Moon be our prosperity, Fame our radiant face, the Mountain our teacher, and the Sky our long life.
The pair of *na* syllables and the third letter *ma* [are placed] upon that;
following the one called *bhujaga*, it is known by the name *Śiśubhṛt*.
Victorious is Kṛṣṇa, who has conquered the lord of the Daityas, whose feet are praised by the gods, and who displays the grace of an emerald within the ocean.
That meter in which there are the syllables *bha*, *ma*, *sa*, and likewise a heavy syllable (*guru*),
is called by the name *rukmavatī*.
May the two jar-like breasts of Śrī, which bestow all the splendor of the deer-marked moon through their own form,
grant you security at the gateway.
Who is that infallible god who is the end-maker?
That meter in which there is a pair of *ra* (short syllables), a *ja* (long syllable), and two *ga*s (heavy syllables),
consisting of eleven syllables, they call the *indravajrā*.
He who, like Mount Mandara, extracted the nectar of fame from the midst of the ocean of battle with the Daitya lords and bestowed it upon the gods with his arm.
May that four-armed one protect you from misfortune.
That meter in which there is a 'ja' syllable, a 'ta' syllable, and a 'ja' syllable joined with a 'ra',
is called Vaṃśastha.
Victorious are the dust-particles from the lotus-feet of Śauri, which are colored by the rays of the crest-jewels of the lords of the gods,
and by the power of contact with which they become purified.
The river Surasravantī bears flowing waters.
That meter in which there are the syllables *ma*, *na*, *ja*, and *ra*, with a heavy syllable (*guru*) likewise [at the end],
and which consists of eleven and three [syllables] respectively, is the *praharṣiṇī*.
May that Lord, who achieved invincible victory over Agni through the prowess of his arms and by whom this earth was swallowed and rendered free of thorns,
grant you perpetual auspiciousness.
A rain-cloud for the waters of the lotus-faces of the Daitya women.
That meter in which there is the letter *ta*, the letter *bha*, two *ja*s, and two heavy syllables (*guru*) is called Vasantatilakā.
To him who, having placed the king of mountains in the midst of the ocean, built a bridge for the sake of harassing the Ten-necked one—
that [Rāma], who is bold in granting the gift of fearlessness to all the worlds—
Homage to the one who wields the circle of staff-like arms, the infallible Acyuta.
Where there is a pair of *na*s, a *ma*, and likewise a pair of *ya*s,
with pauses after the eighth and seventh syllables respectively, that is considered *Mālinī*.
May my speech remain attached to your praise even for a moment;
may my body become solely intent on prostrating before you;
and may it rain down the nectar of knowledge that destroys the defects of worldly existence.
My mind, too, shall always remember you.
Where there is the letter *na*, the letter *ja*, the letter *bha*, and two *ra*s with a heavy syllable (*guru*),
that is the *mālinī* meter, which is highly esteemed by the wise.
[Salutations] to the one whose form reclines upon a couch that is the body of the king of pythons,
who finds delight in the lotus-like hand of the Daughter of the Ocean,
and whose fingers are colored by the luster of the jewels in the crown of the Lord of the Gods.
May the pair of feet of the Enemy of Madhu always stand for your welfare.
That which has "na," "bha," "na," "sa," "ma," "bha," "na," "ta," and two "ga"s is called Mandākrāntā;
in it, the pause occurs after the fourth, sixth, and seventh syllables.

May that Lord, who possesses the form of the Man-Lion, protect us— he whose claws, resembling the inner petals of the *ketakī* flower, scratched the sky as they struck the chest of the enemy of the Lord of the Gods (Indra), which was like a diamond; he who is the jewel of the sky, manifesting his power.
May [the Lord], whose row of filaments is radiant with a mass of rising splendor, purify us.

The *vṛtta* known as *kusumitā* consists of the meters *bhava*, *naya*, *pakāra*, and *yakāra* [as its constituent units], with pauses (*yati*) at the fifth, sixth, and seventh syllables; beyond this, it is called *calitāvellitā*.
May that Keśava protect you— he who assumed the form of a boar, coiled with creepers, which clung to the earth as it was submerged somewhere within the depths of the ocean in order to lift it up.
On his back [or: on his well-nourished body], bearing the grace of leaf-designs made of musk upon the tips of his fangs,
he carries the burden of the earth.
He was gazed upon by the worlds with prostrations performed.
The meter consisting of two *ma*s, two *ja*s, two *ta*s, and a *ga* (with a pause at the twelfth and seventh syllables),
which follows the Śārdūlavikrīḍita, is called Vīkriḍita.
In her hand, there is the constant gathering of flowers for the purpose of worship;
in her eyes, there is the focused meditation upon the pair of lotus feet of the glorious Mādhava;
and in her mind, there is the latent desire to propitiate Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by the arising of intense joy.
May my profuse prattle consist only of the words "Keśava, Keśava."
The *vṛtta* named Sumadanā (or Suvadana), consisting of the syllables *bha*, *ra*, *u*, *bha*, *ra*, *u*, *ya*, *kā*, *ru*, *bha*, *u*, with a pause (*yati*) at the seventh and sixth syllables,
has been proclaimed by poets in their works.
That sovereignty which was born from the arm of Brahmā, uniquely skilled in protecting the world,
passed entirely into the two arms of him who,
having conquered and bestowed the earth upon Himavat, made it his own abode within the ocean.
Victorious is that glorious son of Jamadagni, whose fame is as pure as the moon and who delights in the destruction of Kumbha.
After the three [syllables] *ma-rau-bha-sau* (or *na-ya-kārāṇāṃ*) followed by a third [set of three], there is a pause consisting of twenty-one syllables; such a meter is called *Sragdharā*.
He who, assuming the skillful artifice of the guise of a beautiful woman, personally seized the nectar from the hand of the haughty lord of the Daityas amidst a host of gods;
may he, like the seven-rayed fire that burns the forest of the grass of sins, be the root of attaining ultimate welfare.
May Mukunda, the Lord of Lakṣmī, who is worthy of salutation by the entire world, nourish you all.
Where there are two *tarau*, two *bharau* (or *narau*), two *narau*, and two *gau*, with pauses at the tenth and twelfth syllables,
that is the *vṛtta* called *Mandrakṛt* (or *Bhadraka*), established within the *Ākṛti* class of meters.
May that Kaustubha gem on the chest of the Lord, the enemy of Kaiṭabha— which possesses the luster of the petals of a blue lotus and the splendor of fresh sunlight— bestow prosperity upon you.
In the vast autumnal sky, whose surface is devoid of masses of clouds,
he shines clearly like the beloved of the lotus-bride standing at the midpoint of the day.
With the gaṇas na, ja, bha, ja, bha, sa, and bha, followed by two laghus (lo),
it is called Śaṅkarārkavirāma; then, with da, la, and two laghus (lalitaṃ nāma), this is declared to be a *vṛtta* in the *vikṛti* [class].

Victory to Him whose deeds are sung by the wives of Purandara, who has conquered all enemies— the Asuras— and who rests in bliss upon the couch of the lord of serpents, which possesses a luster as pure as the moon.
Having reached the state of facing his hoods with the auspiciousness sought by all the people of the world,
he established his feet upon the peak of the crystal-bearing mountain, filled with a flood of water.
Like a cloud melting into the eye of the sky, you are the world.
That which has *bha*, *ta*, *na*, *sa*, *bha*,
*ta*, *na*, *sa*, *bha*, *bha*, *na*, *ya*, *ya* [in its gaṇas] is the *tanvī* meter;
it consists of two feet, and its pause occurs after five, seven, and twelve syllables.
He is the moon for the lotus-faces of the wives of the Dānavas,
whose nature is to bestow the prosperity he has received;
his palms hold the conch, mace, and lotus.
He who has accomplished the work of the gods with those endowed with wheels (discuses),
whose pair of feet is praised by the lords of gods and sages, and who bestows the essence of the nectar of liberation upon those who have turned away from the sacrificial banners of ritualism.
May Keśavadeva, whose eyes are like lotuses, being pleased, fulfill for you a thousand desired objects.
The metre named *Krauñcapadā* is known to consist of the gaṇas *bha*, *ma*, *au*, *ṣṭau* (or *bhamausbhau*), and four *na*s, followed by a *ga*;
it is composed with pauses at the fifth, fifth, eighth, and seventh [syllables].

The sound of [his] bowstring, entering within the hollows of the ears like the peak of a thunderbolt, causes the lords of the Daityas at the head of the battle to be overcome by a weight of fear, rending their hearts asunder.
